sermon:
## The First Word Is "Come Back"
*Before the visions, before the comfort, a summons*

**Text:** Zechariah 1:1-6 · **Supporting:** Malachi 3:7; Jeremiah 25:11; Lamentations 3:22; Joel 2:13

The exiles were home, and home was rubble. They had crossed the desert from Babylon expecting Jerusalem and found a ruin. The temple was a foundation and a memory. The walls were gaps. And into that thin, tired remnant, in the eighth month of the second year of Darius, 520 BC, a date you can stand on, the first word God speaks is not comfort. It is a command to turn around.

**A God who is provoked, and still calls**
"The LORD was very angry with your fathers" (Zechariah 1:2). That is how it opens. Not "I have missed you." Not "let me make it up to you." The anger is named first, because the people standing in the ruins were the children of the people who built it. Seventy years of exile, exactly what Jeremiah said decades before: "These nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years" (Jeremiah 25:11). The wreckage they were standing in was not an accident of history, not the bad luck of a small nation between empires. It was the long, patient answer to a long unfaithfulness. God wanted them to know that before he comforted them, because comfort that skips the diagnosis is not comfort. It is sedation.

And then the turn, and it comes fast. "Return to me, says the LORD of hosts, and I will return to you" (Zechariah 1:3). The same word runs underneath the whole book, *shuv*, to turn, to come back, to face the other direction. It is the prophets' word for the only motion that matters, the pivot of the whole Old Testament. Malachi would put it the same way to the same exhausted people a generation later: "Return to me, and I will return to you" (Malachi 3:7). The order is not negotiable, and it is not what we expect. He does not say, I will return to you and then you will feel like coming back. He says: you turn, and you will find I have already turned toward you. The return of the people and the return of God are not two transactions. They are one motion seen from two sides.

**The fathers are gone. The word is not.**
Then God does something that should frighten anyone who has ever assumed there was more time. He points to the dead. "Your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, do they live forever?" (Zechariah 1:5). It is a question with a graveyard for an answer. The generation that ignored the prophets is in the ground. The prophets who warned them, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, the men who stood in the gate and were not believed, are in the ground too. Everyone in that old argument is dead. The accusers and the accused, the warners and the warned, all of it settled now under Babylonian dust.

But the word is not dead. "But my words and my statutes, which I commanded my servants the prophets, did they not overtake your fathers?" (Zechariah 1:6). *Overtake.* The word ran them down like a creditor catching a debtor who thought he had escaped. They believed they had outlived the warning, that enough years had passed to make the threat empty, and the warning outlived them. The men died. The sentence landed. The exile they were told would come, came. And here is the mercy buried in the threat, the thing easy to miss in a verse this heavy, the same word that overtook the fathers in judgment is the word now offered to the children as a door. The word that kills when ignored is the word that saves when heeded. It is the same word. The difference is *shuv*.

**We always think we have more time**
This is the part where I stop describing the exiles. I have stood in a pulpit and called my own delay discernment. I have told myself I would deal with the thing later, that the call to return was for the obviously broken, for the people in the back, not for the man holding the microphone. We do not reject the warning. We do something more cowardly. We file it. We treat the warning as a wall we can lean on rather than a door quietly closing. We assume our fathers' God will keep waiting because he kept waiting before, mistaking his patience for indifference and his silence for absence. And one day someone asks of us exactly what God asked of them, where are they now?, and the only honest answer is that the time we were counting on belonged to him all along, and it is shorter than we budgeted.

The remnant standing in the rubble did the thing their fathers would not do. The text records it in two plain words, without fanfare: "they repented" (Zechariah 1:6). That is the whole sermon Zechariah preaches before the first vision opens. Not a program. Not a building campaign, though the temple needed building. Come back. Everything else in this book, the eight visions, the crowned priest, the King on the donkey, the pierced one, the fountain, all of it unfolds out of this first command, and none of it lands on a heart that will not first turn.

And it is the word that finds its full weight at a cross, where the Branch God will name later in this very book takes the overtaking word into his own body. The sentence that ran down the fathers ran instead into him. He was overtaken in our place so the door could stay open. Joel said it and meant it of this God, the God of the second month and the second year and the second chance: he is "gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love" (Joel 2:13). The exiles standing in the ruins did not deserve a first word. He gave them the best one.

Your fathers died. His word did not.

## The Night God Was Not Sleeping
*Eight visions for a remnant that thought the world had moved on*

**Text:** Zechariah 1:7-6:8 · **Supporting:** Psalm 121:4; Zechariah 2:5; Zechariah 4:6; Revelation 6:4

It came in a single night. On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, three months after the call to return, the word of the LORD came to Zechariah, and what came was not one picture but eight. A procession of visions stacked one against the next, each answering a different ache in a people too small to matter. The remnant looked out at a quiet world. Babylon had fallen, Persia ruled under Darius, the nations were at rest, and Jerusalem sat in ruins beneath all of it, forgotten by everyone with power. The visions of that night are God's answer to the worst thought a defeated people can have, worse than the thought that God is angry. The thought that God has lost interest.

**The horses among the myrtle trees**
The first vision sets the question for the whole night. A man on a red horse stands among the myrtle trees in the glen, and behind him red and sorrel and white horses, patrols God has sent to walk the earth. And they make their report: "We have patrolled the earth, and behold, all the earth remains at rest" (Zechariah 1:11). That sounds like good news. It is not. The nations are at peace, comfortable, undisturbed, and Jerusalem lies in ruins beneath that peace, and that arrangement is intolerable to God. The angel cries out the question every grieving believer eventually asks: how long? And the LORD answers with words the text calls "gracious and comforting", "I am exceedingly jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion" and "I am exceedingly angry with the nations that are at ease" (Zechariah 1:14-15). The quiet of the world was never God's contentment. It was the calm of a God who had not yet moved, and was about to.

**A city too big for walls**
Then a man with a measuring line goes out to measure Jerusalem, and an angel runs to stop him. "Jerusalem shall be inhabited as villages without walls, because of the multitude of people and livestock in it" (Zechariah 2:4). The remnant is measuring for a small wall around a small town, the modest defensible perimeter that frightened people always build first. God is measuring for a city too full to wall in. And the protection will not be masonry at all: "I will be to her a wall of fire all around, declares the LORD, and I will be the glory in her midst" (Zechariah 2:5). A wall you cannot build and cannot breach. The visions keep doing exactly this, taking the small, defensive, sensible calculation of frightened people and breaking it wide open. The remnant keeps thinking survival. God keeps talking abundance.

The night runs on, and the visions deepen. The high priest stands accused in filthy garments and the accuser is silenced and the priest reclothed by grace, a whole sermon in itself. A golden lampstand burns on oil it never has to pump, fed straight from two olive trees, and the word lands that the temple will rise "not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts" (Zechariah 4:6). A flying scroll, thirty feet long, carries the curse against the thief and the false swearer across the whole land, sin will not simply be forgiven, it will be confronted. A woman named Wickedness is sealed in a lead-covered basket and carried off on the wings of two women to Shinar, to the plain of Babel, back to the exact place the human rebellion against God first organized itself. And finally four chariots go out to the four winds of heaven, and the patrol that began the night ends it, the Spirit of God set at rest in the north country, the threat from the north finally answered, the work already underway while the world sleeps.

**The God who does not sleep over you**
Here is where I have to stop and confess that I preach a God I do not always believe in at 2 a.m. I have sat with a grieving man and told him God sees, God is at work, God has not abandoned this, and then driven home and lived as though the quiet of my own ruined places meant God had moved on to busier, more important people. We read the silence as absence. We assume that because nothing is happening that we can see, nothing is happening at all. We mistake the stillness of the surface for the stillness of God. And the entire architecture of these eight visions is built, beam by beam, to take that lie apart. "Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep" (Psalm 121:4). The patrols never stopped walking the earth in the dark. The wall of fire was always around the city the remnant thought was undefended. The accuser was already being silenced before the priest knew he was being defended. The oil was already flowing before anyone thought to ask where the strength would come from.

And it runs straight to the cross, where the world again went quiet, a dead teacher, a sealed tomb, a defeated remnant of eleven men behind a locked door on Saturday, every appearance in the world saying God had finally and completely lost. He had not lost. He was never asleep. The horses were already moving in the dark of that Saturday. One of those chariots in Zechariah carries the red horse that John sees again in Revelation, taking peace from the earth (Revelation 6:4), because the God who restrains the nations for the sake of his small people is the same God who will finally ride out and judge them. The quiet you are standing in is not the quiet of a God who forgot. It is the quiet before the chariots move.

God is not asleep over Jerusalem.

## The Accuser Has a Case. God Has a Robe.
*Standing guilty, dressed by grace*

**Text:** Zechariah 3:1-10 · **Supporting:** Job 1:9-11; Romans 8:33; Isaiah 61:10; Revelation 12:10

It is a courtroom, and the defendant has already lost before the scene opens. Joshua the high priest stands before the angel of the LORD, and at his right hand, the prosecutor's place in an ancient court, stands Satan, the Accuser, *ha-satan*, the one whose whole title means the one who brings the charge. He is there to accuse him. And the worst thing about the scene, the thing that makes it unbearable, is that the accusation is true. Joshua stands there "clothed with filthy garments" (Zechariah 3:3), and the Hebrew word is filthier than our English translations are willing to be, garments fouled with excrement, the most defiling thing a person could wear into the presence of God. This is the holiest man in the nation, the one who alone goes in before God on behalf of everyone else, and he is standing in the throne room covered in his own filth, and the prosecutor is not lying.

**The accuser who is not wrong**
Satan's whole vocation is this. The same figure stood before God about Job and said the quiet thing every accusation says underneath the words: he only serves you because it pays. "Does Job fear God for no reason?" (Job 1:9). Strip away the wealth, said the accuser, and the worship goes with it. The accusation is rarely false. That is precisely what makes it powerful, and what makes the accuser so much more dangerous than a liar. A liar you can refute. The accuser does not need to invent your sin. He only needs to read it back to you, accurately, item by item, in the presence of a holy God, and let the accuracy carry it. He is the prosecutor whose evidence is all admissible. Joshua has nothing to say. There is no defense brief on the table. The garments are the evidence, and the evidence is conclusive, and the defendant knows it. He stands there silent in the filth.

**The judge who will not hear it**
And then the defendant says nothing, because the Judge speaks for him. "The LORD said to Satan, 'The LORD rebuke you, O Satan! The LORD who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you. Is not this a brand plucked from the fire?'" (Zechariah 3:2). Notice carefully what God does not do, because the whole gospel is hiding in the omission. He does not argue the facts. He does not say Joshua is innocent. He does not produce a counter-witness or a character reference. He silences the prosecutor on entirely different grounds, choosing. The LORD who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you. The case is not dismissed for lack of evidence. The evidence is all true. The case is dismissed because the Judge has already, sovereignly, before the trial began, decided to whom this filthy man belongs. A brand plucked from the fire, already rescued, already God's, the smoke still on him.

Then the robe. "Remove the filthy garments from him... Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments" (Zechariah 3:4). Watch the hands in that sentence, or rather watch whose hands they are not. Joshua does not wash himself. He does not petition for a probationary period to prove his repentance. He does not earn his way back into the priesthood through a season of demonstrated holiness. Hands he never sees strip the filth off him and dress him in clean linen while he stands there doing nothing but being acted upon. Then a clean turban is set on his head, and the priest is reinstated, not because the priest got clean, but because God clothed him. Isaiah sang the very same thing, and could only sing it because it was a gift and not a wage: "he has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness" (Isaiah 61:10).

**You stand in the same court**
I know that courtroom from the inside, and so do you. I have stood in it covered in things I would not name from a pulpit, with a voice at my right hand reading the list back to me, every item on it accurate, every charge one I could not deny. And the temptation in that exact moment is to do the one thing Joshua could not do and was never asked to do, to argue, to minimize, to explain the circumstances, to promise that I will be cleaner next time so that the robe might feel a little more earned when it comes. It never works. It cannot work, because the accuser is not lying, and you cannot out-argue the truth. The only thing in the universe that silences him is not my defense. It is God's choice. "Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies" (Romans 8:33). The accuser is thrown down at the last not by the spotless record of the saints but "by the blood of the Lamb" (Revelation 12:10), by a robe that someone else's blood paid for.

And that is exactly where this vision was always pointing, in the same chapter. God says, "Behold, I will bring my servant the Branch," and "I will remove the iniquity of this land in a single day" (Zechariah 3:8-9). One day. One Branch. A priest who would one day stand wearing the filthy garments that were not his own, take the accusation that was ours and not his, and answer it not with an argument but with his body, so that the robe we are handed in the courtroom was bought and paid for before it ever touched us. We do not enter the courtroom to be defended. We enter it already chosen, already a brand plucked from the fire, and the robe is already on the way.

The accuser speaks. God removes him.

## The Mountain That Becomes a Plain
*A temple too big, a remnant too small, a Spirit that does not need either*

**Text:** Zechariah 4:1-14 · **Supporting:** Haggai 2:3; 1 Corinthians 1:27; Ezra 3:12; 2 Corinthians 12:9

Zerubbabel had a foundation and an impossible job. When the foundation of the second temple was first laid, the response of the people split down a generational line. The young shouted for joy, and the old men who had seen Solomon's temple in its glory wept aloud, because they remembered what a temple was supposed to be and this was a footprint in the dirt by comparison (Ezra 3:12). Haggai, preaching to those same men, had to ask the cruel and honest question out loud: "Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? How do you see it now? Is it not as nothing in your eyes?" (Haggai 2:3). The temple they were called to build was too large for the strength they had. The remnant looked at the mountain of work and the handful of laborers and the empty treasury and did the math, and the math said no. It always says no.

**The lamp that feeds itself**
Into that arithmetic God gives Zechariah a strange and patient picture. A golden lampstand, and above it a bowl, and from the bowl seven pipes running to seven lamps, and beside it two olive trees pouring oil into the bowl directly through golden channels. No one carries the oil. No one fills the bowl. No priest stands by with a flask to top it off. The light burns on a supply it never has to produce and never has to manage. Zechariah, like us, does not understand, and asks what it means, twice, because the answer is so unexpected he cannot take it in the first time. And the answer is the single line the whole book turns on, the verse that holds up everything around it: "Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts" (Zechariah 4:6). The lamp does not run on the laborers' effort. It does not run on Zerubbabel's resourcefulness or the remnant's stamina. It runs on a supply that comes from outside them, constantly, without their managing it, and never runs dry.

**The mountain talked down to a plain**
Then God turns and addresses the mountain directly, the way you would speak to something far smaller than it claims to be. "Who are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you shall become a plain" (Zechariah 4:7). The obstacle that defined the entire project, the impossibility everyone in the remnant was measuring and re-measuring, is spoken to like it is nothing, like a hill that just has not been told yet that it is leaving. And the promise that follows is specific and personal: the same hands that laid the foundation will set the final stone. "The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also complete it" (Zechariah 4:9). The man who started the impossible thing will live to see the last stone set, the top stone brought out "amid shouts of 'Grace, grace to it!'" (Zechariah 4:7). Not "well done, good worker." Not a monument to the laborers' persistence. Grace. Even the finished temple, dedicated and standing, is credited to grace and not to the strength that lifted the stones.

**Do not despise the day of small things**
And then comes the verse I need more than the remnant did. "For whoever has despised the day of small things shall rejoice, and shall see the plumb line in the hand of Zerubbabel" (Zechariah 4:10). Whoever has despised. God names the actual sin in the room, and it is not the one we would name. The sin is not the smallness of the work. The sin is the contempt for the smallness, the quiet, sophisticated conviction that because a thing is little, it is therefore nothing, and because it is nothing, God surely is not in it. The remnant's danger was never that the temple was small. It was that they would look at the small thing and conclude God had left the building.

I have despised the day of small things from inside ministry, and I have called it wisdom. I have looked at a small church, a small budget, a small Sunday response, a small and unglamorous obedience, and felt the math close in around me, and called my discouragement realism. It is not realism. It is unbelief carrying a calculator. The whole counterfeit assumes the work runs on might and power, on my strength, my resources, my competence, my platform, when God has said as plainly as he says anything that the work runs on his Spirit, and never did run on mine, and was specifically designed not to. "God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong" (1 Corinthians 1:27). The remnant was not too small for the temple. It was exactly the size God prefers to work with, because a remnant that small cannot, when the thing is finished, turn and take the credit. The smallness was not the obstacle. The smallness was the point.

This is the gospel's own shape, top to bottom. The kingdom of God comes into the world as a mustard seed, a baby in a feed trough, a crucified Galilean and eleven frightened men hiding in a borrowed room, the smallest possible beginning, despised by everyone competent and powerful in the empire, and finished by the Spirit and not by might. The same Lord who would not let Zerubbabel trust his own strength said to a weak and afflicted apostle centuries later, "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). Whatever small and unimpressive obedience God has set in front of you this week is not waiting on your strength to finally become possible. It was never going to run on your strength at all. It runs on oil you do not have to pump.

Not by might. By his Spirit.

## Both the Crown and the Altar
*The two offices Israel never let one man hold*

**Text:** Zechariah 6:9-15 · **Supporting:** Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 7:1-3; 2 Chronicles 26:18; 1 Peter 2:9

Israel kept the crown and the altar apart on purpose, and forgetting it once cost a king his health and his throne. When Uzziah, a good king of Judah, grew strong and proud and walked into the temple to burn incense, work that belonged to the priests alone, eighty priests confronted him to his face: "It is not for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to the LORD, but for the priests, the sons of Aaron, who are consecrated to burn incense" (2 Chronicles 26:18). While the words were still in his mouth, leprosy broke out on his forehead, and he left the temple a leper and lived the rest of his life in a separate house, cut off. The line between throne and altar was not Israelite bureaucracy. It was a fence God himself had built. Kings came from the tribe of Judah. Priests came from the tribe of Levi. No one wore both crown and ephod, because no son of Adam was holy enough to be trusted with both at once.

**A crown for a priest**
So watch carefully what God tells Zechariah to do, because it breaks the fence. Take silver and gold from the exiles newly arrived from Babylon, Heldai, Tobijah, Jedaiah, men named in the text, make an elaborate crown, and set it not on the head of Zerubbabel the governor, the descendant of David, the obvious king. Set it on Joshua the high priest's head (Zechariah 6:11). A royal crown on a priest. The fence God built comes down in a single prophetic act. And lest anyone think this is finally about Joshua himself, that Joshua has somehow been promoted into a king, the word of explanation comes immediately and points past him: "Behold, the man whose name is the Branch: for he shall branch out from his place, and he shall build the temple of the LORD" (Zechariah 6:12). The crown on the priest is a sign, a living signpost, pointing past the priest to a coming man it actually fits.

Then the sentence Israel had kept carefully separate for a thousand years, said now as a promise. "It is he who shall build the temple of the LORD and shall bear royal honor, and shall sit and rule on his throne. And there shall be a priest on his throne, and the counsel of peace shall be between them both" (Zechariah 6:13). A priest on his throne. One man, ruling and interceding at the same time, wearing the crown and tending the altar, and between the two offices that had been kept apart on pain of leprosy, peace. Not the old tension. Not the protective fence. The counsel of peace, because for the first time in the history of the world both offices belong to one person actually worthy of both.

**Why the fence existed**
The fence existed because of a hard truth about power and holiness. Power without holiness destroys, and holiness without authority cannot save. A king who is not a priest will, given enough time, use the people for himself, because he answers to no altar. A priest who is no king can plead for the people and intercede for the people, but he cannot bring in the kingdom the people actually need rescuing into, because he holds no throne. Israel's whole long history is, in one sense, the wreckage of men who held one office and grasped at the other. Uzziah reached for the altar and was struck with leprosy. Saul, impatient before a battle, offered the sacrifice he was forbidden to offer and lost the kingdom from his line. Even good kings could not be priests, and faithful priests could not be kings. The two had to stay apart, generation after generation, because no son of Adam could be trusted to be both at once without one office corrupting the other.

**The man who was worthy of both**
And then, finally, there was one who could. David, who had no business being a priest, sang under inspiration of a son of his who would be: "The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind, 'You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek'" (Psalm 110:4). Melchizedek, that strange and shadowy figure who appears in Genesis as king of Salem and priest of God Most High at the same time, both offices in one man, centuries before the fence was ever built around Aaron's sons. The book of Hebrews spends an entire chapter on him for exactly this reason: he is the pattern, the preview, the precedent for the one who fulfills Zechariah's vision. "He is without father or mother or genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life... he continues a priest forever" (Hebrews 7:3). The Branch is the king-priest the fence was always pointing toward by keeping the offices apart.

I have wanted my leaders to be one thing or the other, a king who will fix the situation by force, or a priest who will only comfort me inside it, and I have been let down by every man who could be only one, including the man in my own mirror. We keep electing kings to be our saviors and ordaining priests to be our comfort, and both keep failing us in the end, because the office we actually need belongs to a man who could not be found among us. He has now come. The Branch arrived, built a temple not made with hands out of living stones, mounted his throne by way of a Roman cross, and at this hour bears royal honor at the right hand of God and intercedes for his people at the same time, the crown and the altar finally in one set of pierced hands.

And the strangest mercy in the whole vision is the last line, the one that reaches across the centuries and lands on outsiders like us. "Those who are far off shall come and help to build the temple of the LORD" (Zechariah 6:15). You, far off, a Gentile, an outsider to the covenant, no descendant of Aaron or Judah, are conscripted into the priesthood of this King. "You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession" (1 Peter 2:9). Royal and priestly, both words, because they belong to the King who is both. The crown and the altar are his alone. And he shares them with the far-off.

One man, both crown and altar.

## The Fast God Never Asked For
*Religion performed at the self, and the justice he actually wanted*

**Text:** Zechariah 7:1-8:23 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 58:6-7; Micah 6:8; Amos 5:21; Matthew 23:23

A delegation comes from Bethel with a sincere religious question, the kind of question good churchgoers ask. For seventy years they have kept a fast in the fifth month, mourning the destruction of the temple Nebuchadnezzar burned, and another in the seventh month, mourning the murder of Gedaliah. Now the temple is rising again under Zerubbabel. The crisis that started the fasting is ending. So they ask the practical question: "Should I weep and abstain in the fifth month, as I have done for so many years?" (Zechariah 7:3). It is an honest question. It is a sincere one. And God's answer is neither a yes nor a no. It is an exposure.

**A fast aimed at the wrong audience**
"When you fasted and mourned in the fifth month and in the seventh, for these seventy years, was it for me that you fasted? And when you eat and when you drink, do you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?" (Zechariah 7:5-6). Was it for me. Seventy years of disciplined, scheduled, religious mourning, and God's first question is whether he was ever the point of any of it. The fast that looked from the outside like devotion was, all along, a fast performed at themselves, their grief, their loss, their wounded national pride, their cherished memory of better days before the empire came. They were the audience for their own piety. God was in the building they wept over, but he was never in the question. He watched seventy years of fasting that had nothing to do with him.

This is the oldest counterfeit in the life of faith, and it is the one I am personally best at. I have performed sorrow over my sin that was, underneath, really sorrow over my reputation. I have given up things, disciplined myself, gone through the motions of seeking God, for the relief I would feel afterward, the standing I would keep, the self-image I was quietly protecting, and called the whole exercise seeking the Lord. The question lands on me before it ever lands on the delegation from Bethel: was it for me that you did it? Because worship that is secretly aimed at the self is not a lesser worship. It is not worship at all. It is the most religious form of selfishness there is, and it can run for seventy years without anyone, including the worshiper, noticing.

**What he asked for instead, and they would not give**
And God reminds them what he had actually asked for all along, in the very words the earlier prophets had used and their fathers had ignored on the way into exile. "Render true judgments, show kindness and mercy to one another, do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner, or the poor, and let none of you devise evil against another in your heart" (Zechariah 7:9-10). That is the fast God wanted. Not the abstaining from food in the fifth month. The justice every day. It is Isaiah's complaint to the same kind of people, almost word for word: "Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness... to share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house?" (Isaiah 58:6-7). It is Micah's entire law compressed into a single line: "to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God" (Micah 6:8). And the fathers' answer to all of it, the answer that sent them into exile, is the saddest sentence in the chapter: "they refused to pay attention and turned a stubborn shoulder and stopped their ears that they might not hear" (Zechariah 7:11). They turned the shoulder a man turns when he has decided to walk away from a conversation. So the great anger came, and the land was made desolate, and they went to Babylon, and now their children are fasting over the rubble their fathers' deafness produced.

**The mourning that becomes a feast**
But God does not leave the people standing in the indictment, and this is the turn that makes it gospel and not merely rebuke. Chapter eight is a stack of "thus says the LORD" promises, one after another after another, and every one of them is return. "I have returned to Zion and will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem" (Zechariah 8:3). Old men and old women will again sit in the streets of the city, each leaning on a staff for great age, in peace, and those same streets will be full of boys and girls playing (Zechariah 8:4-5). After the war and the exile and the rubble, ordinary old age and ordinary childhood, which is its own kind of miracle. And then the fast itself is transformed at the root: "The fast of the fourth month and the fast of the fifth and the fast of the seventh and the fast of the tenth shall be to the house of Judah seasons of joy and gladness and cheerful feasts" (Zechariah 8:19). The God who exposed their hunger as self-serving does not abolish the day. He converts it. The mourning becomes a feast. The mourning was never what he wanted from them in the first place. The joy was.

Centuries later a teacher stood in the courts of the rebuilt temple and said the same thing to people who tithed the herbs in their garden down to the last mint leaf while ignoring the poor at their gate: "You have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others" (Matthew 23:23). The same three concerns, almost the same three words Zechariah used. Justice. Mercy. Faithfulness. And then he did the very fast God had always wanted and Israel had always dodged, he loosed the bonds of the oppressed, he fed the hungry on a hillside, he lifted up the fatherless and welcomed the sojourner, and at the last he gave his own body as the bread shared with a starving world. The feast Zechariah promised the exiles is set on a table he bought with his life. The mourning is over because the Shepherd took it.

He wanted justice, not your hunger.

## The King Who Comes Too Low to Fear
*Salvation that arrives on a borrowed donkey*

**Text:** Zechariah 9:9-17 · **Supporting:** Matthew 21:5; Isaiah 53:2; Philippians 2:8; John 18:36

The nations announced their kings with cavalry. A conqueror came into a captured city on a war-horse, with chariots rolling behind him and the smoke of the last battle still on his clothes, and the city understood instantly and without a word what kind of king had arrived and exactly what he was going to cost them. That was the visual grammar of power in the ancient world, the language every empire spoke. It has not changed as much as we like to think. Strength rides high. Strength rides armed. Strength makes you afraid on purpose, because fear is how it rules. And into that grammar, into a world that knew only that kind of king, Zechariah drops a single sentence that breaks the language apart.

**Behold, and then the anticlimax**
"Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! Shout aloud, O daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your king is coming to you" (Zechariah 9:9). *Behold*, the word that announces the war-horse, the word that makes a city look up and brace itself. The crowd tenses for the cavalry. And then the king the verse goes on to describe is everything the war-horse is not. "Righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey" (Zechariah 9:9). A donkey. Not a stallion. Not a chariot. Not even a horse. The animal a man rides when he comes in peace, the plodding domestic animal that cannot charge, that was never bred for battle, that announces by its very gait that no war is coming. The verse holds together two things the world has always insisted cannot occupy the same king: a king who actually brings salvation, real rescue, real victory, and a king too low and too gentle to be afraid of.

**The king who disarms his own city**
And watch what this strange king does with the weapons, because it is the opposite of every conqueror who ever lived. The conqueror seizes the city's arms in order to control it, to make resistance impossible. This king destroys the arms in order to free it. "I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the war-horse from Jerusalem; and the battle bow shall be cut off, and he shall speak peace to the nations" (Zechariah 9:10). Read it slowly. He does not confiscate Jerusalem's weapons to leave Jerusalem helpless and dependent on him. He cuts off Jerusalem's own war-machine because in the place where he reigns it is simply not needed anymore. The chariot, the war-horse, the battle bow, the whole apparatus of self-protection, gone, not because he has disarmed his enemies but because he has disarmed his own people, having made their weapons obsolete. His dominion runs "from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth" (Zechariah 9:10), and it runs that far not on cavalry but on a word of peace. This is a king whose total victory does not resemble any victory the nations have ever celebrated.

**The Messiah we did not order**
Five centuries after Zechariah wrote it, a man rode that exact route into that exact city on that exact animal. Matthew quotes this verse the way you quote a prophecy you are watching come true in front of your face: "Say to the daughter of Zion, 'Behold, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey'" (Matthew 21:5). The crowds lining the road were thrilled, waving branches, shouting Hosanna, and they were thrilled because they read the donkey wrong. They wanted the war-horse hidden somewhere inside it. They wanted the humble entrance to be a clever prelude, the gentle opening move before the cavalry charge that would finally throw Rome out of Jerusalem. They cheered a Messiah they had not actually been promised. And by Friday of that same week they had turned on him and called for his blood, because he kept being the donkey all the way down to the end. He told Pilate plainly, with a Roman execution hours away, "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews" (John 18:36). No fighting. No charge. The battle bow stayed cut off, in his own hand, at his own unbearable cost.

And I have to be honest about which king I keep waiting for, because the crowd's mistake is my own. I want the one on the war-horse. I want the God who will come into my situation armed and decisive, who will end my enemies and remove every threat and make my fear unnecessary by sheer overwhelming force. The donkey embarrasses me. A king "humble and mounted on a donkey" cannot be conscripted into my campaigns or deployed against the people I would like to see defeated. He will not be drafted into my outrage. He refuses to ride at the front of the army I keep trying to raise. Isaiah saw this King coming from far off and warned us in advance that we would not be impressed, that we would in fact look right past him: "he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him" (Isaiah 53:2). We priced the donkey as weakness, every one of us, the way the Friday crowd did when the gentle King refused to become the violent one they had cheered on Sunday. It was the throne. The donkey was the throne the whole time. "He humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross" (Philippians 2:8). The lowest possible mount carried the highest possible King to the lowest possible place, the cross, and that, precisely that, is how he won the whole earth from sea to sea. Not by taking up the weapons we wanted in his hands, but by refusing every single one of them, and dying instead.

The King comes low, on a donkey.

## The Price of a Slave
*What it costs a people to value their Shepherd at nothing*

**Text:** Zechariah 11:4-17 · **Supporting:** Exodus 21:32; Matthew 27:9-10; John 10:11; Psalm 41:9

This is the dark chapter of the book, and it is meant to be dark. God commissions the prophet to act out a parable with his own body and his own labor. "Thus said the LORD my God: Become shepherd of the flock doomed to slaughter" (Zechariah 11:4). He is to shepherd a people who have been sold out by their own leaders, "those who buy them slaughter them and go unpunished, and those who sell them say, Blessed be the LORD, I have become rich" (Zechariah 11:5). The leaders are fattening the flock for the kill and thanking God for the profit. So the prophet takes up the doomed flock, takes two shepherd's staffs, names one Favor and one Union, and tends the sheep no one else would tend. And it ends in rejection so total that it can only be measured in a sum of money.

**Thirty pieces of silver**
The prophet wearies of the flock and the flock detests him in return, and so the relationship breaks. He breaks the staff called Favor, annulling the covenant of protection. And then he asks the people for his wages, and in that single moment the parable becomes one of the most precise predictive prophecies in the entire Old Testament. "Then I said to them, 'If it seems good to you, give me my wages; but if not, keep them.' And they weighed out as my wages thirty pieces of silver" (Zechariah 11:12). Thirty pieces of silver. That number is not a random figure, and no Israelite hearing it would have missed the insult buried in it. The law of Moses had fixed that exact amount as the legal value of a slave killed by someone's ox: "If the ox gores a slave, male or female, the owner shall give to their master thirty shekels of silver" (Exodus 21:32). Thirty shekels was the compensation you paid for a dead slave. That is what they weighed out for the shepherd God had given them. Not an insult thrown out in anger. An appraisal, calmly arrived at. They looked at the man God sent to shepherd their souls, set him on the scale, and priced him at the going rate for replacing a slave the ox had gored.

**Thrown to the potter, in the house of the LORD**
And then comes God's own verdict on the wage, dripping with a bitterness the translators can barely contain. "Throw it to the potter, the lordly price at which I was priced by them" (Zechariah 11:13). The lordly price. Said in the most savage irony in the prophets. So the prophet takes the thirty pieces of silver and throws them down, in the house of the LORD, to the potter. The silver clatters across the temple floor where God dwells. Then he breaks the second staff, the one called Union, "annulling the brotherhood between Judah and Israel" (Zechariah 11:14). The logic is exact and terrible: a people who price their shepherd at slave-cost do not get to keep their unity as a gift. The bonds come apart. And the chapter ends with the worst image of all, a worthless shepherd raised up in the good shepherd's place, a leader who "does not care for those being destroyed," who eats the flesh of the fat sheep, whose arm withers and whose right eye goes blind (Zechariah 11:15-17). This is the wage of the rejection. Refuse the true shepherd and you do not end up with no shepherd at all. You end up with a false one who devours you.

**We weighed him too**
Matthew saw exactly where this prophecy was always going, and he said so without flinching. When Judas, sick with what he had done, threw the thirty pieces of silver back into the temple, and the chief priests scrupled to put blood money in the treasury and used it instead to buy a potter's field as a burial ground for strangers, Matthew wrote: "Then was fulfilled what had been spoken by the prophet Jeremiah, saying, 'And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him on whom a price had been set... and they gave them for the potter's field'" (Matthew 27:9-10). Thirty pieces of silver. The potter. The house of the LORD. Five hundred years early, down to the coin and the field. The Good Shepherd who stood in Jerusalem and said "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep" (John 10:11) was sold by one of his own for the price the law set on a dead slave, and the one who sold him was a friend who had shared his table, "even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me" (Psalm 41:9).

It is comfortable to lay the whole betrayal on Judas and walk away from the chapter feeling clean. I cannot do it, and neither can you. I have priced the Shepherd cheap in my own currency more times than I would say from a pulpit, given him the leftover end of my week, the spare attention after everything urgent was handled, the offering I would not actually miss, and quietly called it devotion. We all set a number on Christ, every one of us, whether or not we ever count out the coins. The number is not what we say about him on Sunday. The number is what he is worth on the ordinary days when no one is watching and following him would cost something real and unrecovered. They weighed him in the temple and the scale read thirty, the price of a goring. The terror of this chapter is how often, on those quiet days, mine reads about the same. And the unbearable mercy underneath the terror is this, the Shepherd they appraised at slave-price let himself be sold at slave-price, willingly, so that the slaves doomed for slaughter could be bought back, not for thirty pieces of silver, but at the price of his own blood.

They weighed the Shepherd at slave price.

## They Will Look on the One They Pierced
*The mourning that comes before the cleansing*

**Text:** Zechariah 12:1-13:1 · **Supporting:** John 19:34-37; Revelation 1:7; Ezekiel 36:26; Romans 2:4

God introduces himself before he says the hard thing, and the introduction is not decoration, it is the ground the hard thing stands on. "Thus declares the LORD, who stretched out the heavens and founded the earth and formed the spirit of man within him" (Zechariah 12:1). The one who is about to speak is the one who stretched out the heavens like a tent, who laid the foundation of the earth, who reached into the human chest and formed the spirit inside it. Remember who is talking. Because what he is about to say is that he intends to break a nation's heart, and only the Creator who formed that heart in the first place has both the right and the tenderness to break it the right way.

**A spirit of grace and pleading**
The chapter promises that on a coming day, when the nations gather against Jerusalem like a heavy stone, God himself will defend his people, the feeblest among them on that day shall be like David, and the house of David shall be like God, like the angel of the LORD going before them (Zechariah 12:8). And then, right in the middle of a battle scene, God abruptly turns the action inward, away from the gathered armies and into the human heart. "And I will pour out on the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy" (Zechariah 12:10). Before they mourn, he gives them the spirit that makes mourning possible. The grief that is about to come is not something they work up in themselves by religious effort. It is poured out on them from above. Repentance here, as everywhere in Scripture if we are honest about it, is a gift before it is ever a response. Ezekiel, preaching to the same exiled people, said it just as plainly: "I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh" (Ezekiel 36:26). The heart of stone cannot mourn. It is too hard to break. God has to give a new one first, and only then can the tears come.

**They look on the one they pierced**
Then comes the sentence the whole chapter is built around, and it changes pronouns mid-clause in a way that has occupied translators and theologians for two thousand years, because the grammar itself is staggering and refuses to be tidied up. "And they shall look on me, on him whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child, and weep bitterly over him, as one weeps over a firstborn" (Zechariah 12:10). They shall look on me, God is speaking, in the first person. Whom they have pierced, and now, in the same breath, it is him, a third person, the wounded one. The LORD who speaks and the pierced one they mourn are somehow, impossibly, the same person. And the mourning is the deepest grief the ancient world knew how to name: the death of an only child, the loss of a firstborn son, the future itself cut off. The land mourns family by family, the text says, each clan by itself, the house of David apart, the house of Nathan apart, the house of Levi apart, the family of Shimei apart, and all their wives by themselves (Zechariah 12:12-14). This is not crowd grief, the easy collective sorrow that asks nothing of anyone. It is each household, alone, each person isolated with what they personally did to him.

**The fountain opens at the lowest point**
And here is the order of events, and the order is the entire gospel. The cleansing does not come before the mourning to make the mourning unnecessary. It comes after. "On that day there shall be a fountain opened for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, to cleanse them from sin and uncleanness" (Zechariah 13:1). On that day, the day they look on the pierced one and finally break. The fountain opens at the very bottom of the grief, not floating safely above it. And here is the wonder that should put a hand over every mouth: the very sin that pierced him becomes the very sin the fountain washes away. They wound the one who turns out to be their only cleansing, and instead of destroying them for it, he cleanses them of the wounding. The blood they drew opens as the fountain that washes them clean of having drawn it.

John stood at the foot of the cross and watched this verse happen with his own eyes. "But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water." And John, who knew his Zechariah by heart, immediately reached for it: "For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled... And again another Scripture says, 'They will look on him whom they have pierced'" (John 19:34-37). Blood and water flowing from a pierced side. The fountain of chapter thirteen, opened on a hill outside the city wall. And Revelation tells us the looking is not finished, that there is a final day of it still coming: "Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him" (Revelation 1:7).

I do not get to read this prophecy as ancient history about other people's hands and other people's spears. The piercing was not accomplished only by a Roman soldier doing his job on a Friday afternoon. It is the kindness of God that leads a person to repentance (Romans 2:4), and the kindness here is both brutal and merciful at the same time. He pours out the spirit of grace that finally lets me see my own hands on the spear, my own sin in the wound. The mourning Zechariah describes is not despair, and it is not the end. It is the only door to the fountain. You cannot be washed clean in a fountain you will not admit your own hands opened.

They look on the one they pierced.

## The Fire That Leaves a People
*A fountain to wash them, a sword to strike the Shepherd, a furnace to make a remnant*

**Text:** Zechariah 13:1-9 · **Supporting:** Matthew 26:31; 1 Peter 1:7; Malachi 3:3; Hosea 2:23

The fountain is open. That is where this chapter begins, picking up the last words of the one before it, "On that day there shall be a fountain opened for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, to cleanse them from sin and uncleanness" (Zechariah 13:1), and everything that follows is what an opened fountain actually does to a land. It does not only wash. It clears. When the true source of cleansing finally arrives, the counterfeits have to go, every one of them, and the chapter moves through three hard and glorious things in order: the idols cut off, the Shepherd struck, the remnant refined.

**The idols and the false prophets, cut off**
First the cleansing turns on the lies that competed with God for the people's trust. "I will cut off the names of the idols from the land, so that they shall be remembered no more. And also I will remove from the land the prophets and the spirit of uncleanness" (Zechariah 13:2). The false prophets are dealt with so completely that the trade itself becomes a thing to hide. A man who once prophesied lies will deny he ever did it, even his own parents will run him through if he keeps it up, and a man with the ritual self-inflicted marks of a pagan prophet on his body will claim they are ordinary wounds, "the wounds I received in the house of my friends" (Zechariah 13:6). He lies even about the evidence of his lying. The point is severe and clean: a polluted prophet and a pure fountain cannot share a land. One of them has to go, and God says without hesitation which one it will be.

**Strike the Shepherd**
And then comes the verse that should make us put a hand over our mouths, because the sword does not fall where we expect it. It does not fall on the false prophet here. It falls on the true one. "Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, against the man who stands next to me, declares the LORD of hosts. Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered" (Zechariah 13:7). The man who stands next to me, the LORD's own companion, the true Shepherd of the earlier chapters, the very one priced at thirty pieces of silver and rejected. And the command from heaven is not to defend him but to strike him. God himself wakes the sword against his own Shepherd. The scattering of the sheep that follows is not an accident or a tragic side effect; it is the consequence God names out loud, in advance, as part of the plan. The Shepherd is struck on purpose, and the flock scatters on purpose, and God is the one who said both would happen.

Jesus quoted this exact verse on the last night of his life, walking out to the Mount of Olives after the supper, and told his men precisely what was about to happen to all of them. "You will all fall away because of me this night. For it is written, 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered'" (Matthew 26:31). He knew the sword was coming for him. He knew, and this is the part that undoes me, that it was the Father's sword and not merely the soldiers'. And he walked straight into it on purpose, so that the strike that should by every right have scattered us forever fell on him instead, and gathered us in the end.

**The third brought through the fire**
And then comes the furnace. The numbers are stark and not softened. Two-thirds of the land is cut off and perishes, "and the third part shall be left alive. And I will put this third into the fire, and refine them as one refines silver, and test them as gold is tested" (Zechariah 13:8-9). Notice that the surviving third is not exempt from the fire. The surviving third is what the fire produces. The silver-refiner of the ancient world sat over his crucible and watched the molten metal, and he did not pull it out the moment it was uncomfortable for the silver; he kept it in the heat, skimming the dross off the top, until he could finally see his own face reflected clean in the surface. That was how he knew it was done. Malachi, preaching to these very same returned exiles, used the identical picture of the coming Lord: "he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver" (Malachi 3:3). The fire is not God's abandonment of his remnant. It is the proof of his attention to it. He sits over the crucible. He does not walk away.

And I have to confess that I want the fountain without the furnace. I want to be washed and then comfortably left alone, cleansed and then untroubled. I have prayed, more times than I would admit from a pulpit, eagerly for the cleansing and quietly against the refining, as though I could keep the gold and skip the very fire that makes the gold gold. The chapter will not let me have it both ways. The same God who opens the fountain in verse one wakes the sword in verse seven and lights the furnace in verse nine, and he does all three with the same hand and the same love, because he is making a people and not merely pardoning a crowd. "The tested genuineness of your faith, more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire, may be found to result in praise and glory and honor" (1 Peter 1:7).

And listen to what the whole fire is finally for, because it is the entire point and it lands on the sweetest words in all the prophets. The refined remnant comes out the far side of the furnace, and "they will call upon my name, and I will answer them. I will say, 'They are my people'; and they will say, 'The LORD is my God'" (Zechariah 13:9). That is Hosea's promise, the broken covenant put back together, the names reversed: "I will say to Not My People, 'You are my people'; and he shall say, 'You are my God'" (Hosea 2:23). The struck Shepherd, the scattered sheep, the consuming fire, all of it, every hard thing in the chapter, ends in a Shepherd who has a people again, on the far side of a furnace, God and his refined remnant calling each other by name. The fire was never the end. The people are.

Struck Shepherd, scattered sheep, cleansed remnant.

## When Even the Pots Are Holy
*The day the LORD stops being one God among the city's many*

**Text:** Zechariah 14:1-21 · **Supporting:** Revelation 11:15; Acts 1:11-12; Philippians 2:10-11; Revelation 21:22-23

The book ends exactly where it has been heading the whole way through, a day. "Behold, a day is coming for the LORD" (Zechariah 14:1). And it opens at the worst possible moment, when everything appears finally and completely lost. The nations are gathered against Jerusalem, the city is taken, the houses are plundered, the women are violated, and half the people are already marched out into exile (Zechariah 14:2). It reads like every other defeat in Israel's long and bitter history, the same old ending the empires always wrote. And then the single sentence that breaks the whole pattern Israel had come to expect: "Then the LORD will go out and fight against those nations as when he fights on a day of battle" (Zechariah 14:3). The remnant does not rally and turn the tide by its own courage. There is no heroic last stand. God himself takes the field.

**His feet on the mountain**
And then a detail so concrete it stops you cold. "On that day his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives that lies before Jerusalem on the east, and the Mount of Olives shall be split in two from east to west by a very wide valley" (Zechariah 14:4). Feet. The God who stretched out the heavens has feet, and those feet stand on a specific, named hill just east of the city, and the mountain itself splits open under them into a valley of escape for the trapped people. The whole vision insists on the physical and the particular, feet, a named mountain, a valley running east and west, living waters that "shall flow out from Jerusalem, half of them to the eastern sea and half of them to the western sea" in summer and in winter alike (Zechariah 14:8). A river that does not run dry when the rains stop. This is not a spiritualized abstraction floating somewhere above history. It is a King with real feet planted on a real hill outside a real city.

Two men in white robes once stood on that very hill and promised those feet would come back to it. When Jesus had finished speaking to his disciples and was lifted up into the cloud from the Mount of Olives, the two angels told the staring men: "This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven" (Acts 1:11). And Luke is careful to name the place they were standing, they "returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem" (Acts 1:12). The same mountain in both Testaments. The feet that left from Olivet are the feet that will stand on it.

**One LORD, one name**
Then comes the verse the whole Old Testament has been straining and reaching toward since Sinai. "And the LORD will be king over all the earth. On that day the LORD will be one and his name one" (Zechariah 14:9). Not the king of one small city in the hills. Not one tribal god holding his ground in the lineup of the nations' many gods. King over all the earth, the LORD one and his name one. Israel had confessed "the LORD our God, the LORD is one" for centuries, the Shema recited morning and evening, but here it stops being a creed they whisper to themselves against the surrounding idols and becomes a public fact the whole earth is forced to reckon with at last. John heard the same trumpet sound and reported it: "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever" (Revelation 11:15). And Paul wrote the certainty of it to a small church under a different empire: "at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord" (Philippians 2:10-11). One LORD. One name. Confessed everywhere.

**Holy to the LORD, on the cooking pots**
And here is how the book chooses to end, and it is not with thunder or with armies. It ends with kitchenware. On that day, the inscription once engraved on a single gold plate worn on the high priest's forehead alone, "Holy to the LORD", will be written on the bells of the horses (Zechariah 14:20). And not only the horses. "And every pot in Jerusalem and Judah shall be holy to the LORD of hosts, so that all who sacrifice may come and take of them and boil the meat of the sacrifice in them" (Zechariah 14:21). Common cooking pots, the most ordinary objects in the house, holy enough that anyone bringing a sacrifice can take one off the shelf and use it for the altar. The line between sacred and ordinary, the line the entire temple system existed for centuries to guard and police, simply dissolves. The horse's harness is holy. The household pot is holy. There is no profane left, because there is no longer any place in the city where the LORD is not King.

That is the future this small, tired, frightened remnant, rebuilding a ruined temple stone by stone, weeping at how little it was, was handed by God. And it is the future I keep quietly dividing back up into zones. I keep a sacred hour and a profane week. A holy room and a common ordinary life. A King over my Sunday worship and a self firmly on the throne of my Monday morning. The whole point of the cooking pots, the reason the book lands there of all places, is that he will not be quartered off into the religious section of my life. He will be King over all the earth, harness and pot and every square inch of the ordinary, or he is not yet the King this book has been promising for fourteen chapters. And when he finally is, the temple Zechariah's people wept and labored to rebuild will not even be needed, because the whole city will have become the holy place: "I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb. And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb" (Revelation 21:22-23). One LORD. One name. Even the pots.

The LORD will be king over all.
